title: What are Java Records (Java 16), what do they auto-generate, and when should you use them vs regular classes?

s1_definition.oneliner: `record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {}` = immutable, auto equals/hashCode/toString, accessor methods id()/amount(). Use for DTOs and value objects. Java 16+.
s1_definition.profdef: A `record` is a compact, immutable data carrier class introduced in Java 16. `record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {}` auto-generates: (1) private final fields for each component, (2) canonical constructor, (3) accessor methods (id(), amount() – NOT getId/getAmount), (4) equals() based on all components, (5) hashCode() based on all components, (6) toString() showing all components. Records are final (cannot be extended), cannot have instance fields beyond the components, and components are immutable (final). Use records for DTOs, value objects, tuples, and any class whose identity is defined by its data.
s1_definition.analogy: A record is like a bank receipt: it has fixed fields (date, amount, account), is SEALED (you can't add extra notes after printing), and two receipts with the same data are considered EQUAL. You don't write getDate()/equals()/hashCode()/toString() for every receipt – the receipt PRINTER (compiler) does it automatically.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Record auto-generation:
  ───────────────────────
  record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {}
       │
       ▼ Compiler generates:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ private final String id;            │
  │ private final BigDecimal amount;    │
  │                                     │
  │ Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) │  canonical constructor
  │ String id()                         │  accessor (not getId)
  │ BigDecimal amount()                 │  accessor
  │ boolean equals(Object)              │  all components
  │ int hashCode()                      │  all components
  │ String toString()                   │  all components
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
  Immutable. Final. Thread-safe.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Records (Java 16) are immutable data carriers that auto-generate constructor, accessor methods (id() not getId()), equals, hashCode, and toString from the component declaration. `record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {}` replaces 50+ lines of POJO boilerplate.

Records are final, cannot extend classes, cannot have mutable instance fields, and component accessors use component names (not JavaBean naming). The compact constructor `Trade { validate(); }` enables validation without repeating parameter assignments.

Use records for DTOs, value objects, map keys, events, and any class whose identity is its data. Do not use them where you need mutability, inheritance, or encapsulated behavior-rich domain entities. Records + sealed classes + pattern matching form modern Java's algebraic data types.

Remember one sentence: record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {} replaces 50+ lines of POJO with auto-generated immutable fields, equals, hashCode, and toString.

---

keyPoints: record Trade(String id, BigDecimal amount) {} replaces 50+ lines of POJO with auto-generated constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, toString.
Accessor methods use component names (id(), amount()), not JavaBean convention (getId(), getAmount()).
All fields are private final. Records are immutable, cannot have mutable instance fields, and are implicitly final.
Compact constructor Trade { validate(); } validates without repeating parameter assignments.
Records make excellent Map keys because equals and hashCode are correctly generated from all components.
Records cannot extend classes but can implement interfaces, add static fields, and add instance methods.
Use records for DTOs, value objects, and events. Use regular classes for mutable entities and inheritance.
